whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the UX Designer exam for?

personas.label: UX designers working on Salesforce projects
personas.description: You design user experiences for Salesforce implementations and want to validate your skills in research, wireframing, prototyping, and accessibility.

personas.label: Admins and consultants with design responsibilities
personas.description: You configure Lightning page layouts, Experience Cloud sites, and Dynamic Forms and want formal UX design credentials to complement your platform skills.

personas.label: Product designers transitioning to enterprise platforms
personas.description: You have UX design experience outside Salesforce and want to apply human-centered design methods within the Lightning Design System and Experience Cloud.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the UX Designer Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The UX Designer exam is moderate in difficulty. It tests UX principles and research methods applied to Salesforce — the challenge is knowing both design theory (WCAG, design thinking) and Salesforce-specific tooling (SLDS, Lightning App Builder, Dynamic Forms).
bullets: ~65% passing score — you can miss up to 21 questions.
Design thinking phases — expect questions that describe a UX activity and ask which design thinking phase (Empathise, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test) it belongs to.
Accessibility standards — you need to know WCAG 2.1 AA requirements including colour contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal text), keyboard navigation, and ARIA labels.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Score 75%+ on practice exams and make sure you can map UX activities to design thinking phases and explain the four WCAG principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust).

examFormat.heading: UX Designer Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or in-person. Here is the format:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: About 45-55% of questions are scenario-based. Common patterns include choosing the right research method for a given design question, identifying which WCAG principle applies to an accessibility scenario, and selecting the correct Salesforce UX tool for a page design requirement.
bestWayToPass: Know the design thinking phases: Empathise (user research), Define (problem statement), Ideate (brainstorm), Prototype (build representations), Test (validate with users) — and which artefacts each phase produces.
Master WCAG 2.1 AA standards: Know the POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust), colour contrast ratios, and how the Lightning Design System provides accessible components.

Understand Salesforce UX tooling: Lightning App Builder for page composition, Dynamic Forms for conditional field visibility, Dynamic Actions for contextual button display, and Compact Layouts for record highlights.

Study research methods: Know when to use qualitative methods (interviews, usability testing, contextual inquiry) vs quantitative methods (surveys, analytics, task completion rates), and what card sorting and tree testing validate.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers applying UX research, wireframing, prototyping, and accessibility standards (WCAG 2.1) to design usable experiences within Lightning Experience and Experience Cloud.

keyConcepts.h2: UX Designer: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Design Thinking Process: Five Phases
blocks.body: Design Thinking is the core framework: Empathise (observe users, conduct interviews, develop empathy maps), Define (synthesise research into a problem statement — "How Might We" framing), Ideate (brainstorm solutions without judgment), Prototype (build low-fi or hi-fi representations), Test (validate with real users and iterate). The exam presents a UX activity (e.g., "interviewing stakeholders about pain points") and asks which phase it belongs to.

blocks.heading: UX Research Methods: Qualitative vs Quantitative
blocks.body: Qualitative methods explore the "why": user interviews, contextual inquiry (observing users in their real environment), and moderated usability testing. Quantitative methods measure the "what": surveys, click analytics, and task completion rates. Card sorting tests how users categorise information (used to design navigation). Tree testing validates whether users can find content within a proposed structure. Affinity diagramming groups qualitative findings into themes. Know which method to select for a given research question.

blocks.heading: Wireframes, Prototypes, and the Design Handoff
blocks.body: Low-fidelity wireframes communicate structure, hierarchy, and layout without visual polish — used for early stakeholder alignment. High-fidelity prototypes include visual design, real content, and interactive states — used for usability testing and developer handoff. The design handoff documents component specifications, spacing, and interaction behaviours. In Salesforce context, Experience Builder mockups and flow screens can be designed declaratively before development. Prototyping prevents rework by catching usability issues early.

blocks.heading: Accessibility: WCAG 2.1 and Salesforce SLDS
blocks.body: WCAG 2.1 defines four principles (POUR): Perceivable (text alternatives for non-text content, sufficient colour contrast), Operable (keyboard navigation, no seizure-inducing animations), Understandable (clear labels, error messages, consistent navigation), Robust (compatible with assistive technologies). The Salesforce Lightning Design System (SLDS) provides accessible, pre-built UI components that meet WCAG AA. The exam tests which WCAG principle applies to a given accessibility scenario.

blocks.heading: Salesforce UX Tooling: Lightning App Builder and Dynamic Forms
blocks.body: **Lightning App Builder** enables drag-and-drop page composition — Home, Record, and App pages — using standard and custom components. **Dynamic Forms** move fields and sections from the page layout into the record page, enabling conditional visibility based on field values or user permissions. Dynamic Actions control button visibility with similar logic. Compact Layouts define the fields shown in record highlights, mobile previews, and related lists. Know the difference between **page layouts** (object-level, profile-based) and dynamic forms (page-level, condition-based).

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce UX Designer Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The UX Designer exam tests user experience principles applied to Salesforce implementations. Focus on the Lightning Design System, accessibility standards, user research methods, and how to design usable Salesforce configurations.

blocks.heading: Lightning Design System (SLDS)
blocks.body: Know the SLDS component library, design tokens, utility classes, and how SLDS ensures visual consistency across Salesforce. Understand when to use standard components vs. custom-styled components.

blocks.heading: Accessibility Standards
blocks.body: Know WCAG 2.1 AA requirements: keyboard navigation, screen reader support (ARIA labels), color contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal text), and how to use Salesforce Accessibility Checker to audit Lightning components.

blocks.heading: User Research in Salesforce Projects
blocks.body: Know how to conduct user interviews, usability tests, and card sorting exercises for Salesforce page layout and navigation design. Understand how to translate findings into actionable design recommendations.

blocks.heading: Page Layout & App Design
blocks.body: Know how to design Lightning **page layouts**: component placement, progressive disclosure, and how to use visibility rules to reduce cognitive load. Understand how the **Lightning App Builder** enables no-code page customization.

blocks.heading: Prototyping & Testing
blocks.body: Know how to create wireframes and clickable prototypes for Salesforce configurations using tools like Figma or SLDS prototyping kits. Understand how to run usability tests with real Salesforce users.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Designer Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After this designer certification, consider the other designer cert or Experience Cloud:

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary focus of a Certified UX Designer on the Salesforce Platform?
options: Building and designing human-centered experiences on the Salesforce Platform
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certified UX Designers build and design human-centered experiences on the Salesforce Platform.
whyWrong: 'Only backend' misrepresents UX Design, which is about human-centered front-end experiences, not backend systems.
Email is unrelated to the UX Designer's core experience-design focus.
Slack is unrelated to the UX Designer's core experience-design focus.

sampleQuestions.question: Which principle is central to human-centered design?
options: Understanding user needs, behaviors, and context to design solutions
sampleQuestions.explanation: Human-centered design focuses on user needs, behaviors, and context.
whyWrong: 'Only aesthetics' undersells human-centered design, which is about understanding user needs and behavior, not just visuals.
'Only performance' misattributes the principle to a technical concern, not user understanding.
'Only cost' misattributes the principle to a business concern, not user understanding.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Salesforce capability do UX Designers often work with?
options: Lightning Experience, Experience Cloud, and declarative UI
sampleQuestions.explanation: They work with Lightning Experience, Experience Cloud, and declarative UI.
whyWrong: 'Only Apex' narrows the platform focus incorrectly to a single programming language.
'Only Heroku' undersells the broader set of Salesforce UI capabilities UX Designers work with.
'Only MuleSoft' undersells the broader set of Salesforce UI capabilities UX Designers work with.

sampleQuestions.question: What does accessibility mean in UX design?
options: Designing so that products are usable by people with diverse abilities
sampleQuestions.explanation: Accessibility ensures products are usable by people with diverse abilities.
whyWrong: 'Only speed' misattributes accessibility to a performance concern, not usability for diverse abilities.
'Only mobile' undersells accessibility, which applies across all devices, not just mobile.
'Only desktop' undersells accessibility, which applies across all devices, not just desktop.

sampleQuestions.question: Who is the UX Designer certification for?
options: Aspiring or experienced designers wanting to build human-centered experiences on the Salesforce Platform
sampleQuestions.explanation: It's for aspiring or experienced designers building human-centered experiences on the platform.
whyWrong: 'Only developers' is too narrow — this certification targets designers broadly, not developers.
'Only admins' is too narrow — this certification targets designers, not administrators.
'Only marketers' is too narrow — this certification targets designers, not marketers.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of user research in UX design?
options: To understand user needs, pain points, and behaviors before designing
sampleQuestions.explanation: User research informs design by understanding needs and behaviors.
whyWrong: 'To skip design' is the opposite of user research's purpose, which informs design, not replaces it.
'Only to validate' undersells research's broader purpose, which includes understanding needs upfront, not just validation.
'Only to test' undersells research's broader purpose, which includes understanding needs upfront, not just testing.

sampleQuestions.question: Which deliverable communicates structure and layout before visual design?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Wireframes communicate structure and layout before visual design.
whyWrong: 'Final UI only' is the opposite of wireframes' purpose, which is pre-visual-design structure.
'Code only' misattributes wireframes' purpose to implementation, not structural design communication.
'Reports only' is unrelated to wireframes' structural design purpose.

sampleQuestions.question: What does prototyping support in the design process?
options: Testing and validating design concepts with users before development
sampleQuestions.explanation: Prototypes enable early testing and validation of design concepts.
whyWrong: 'Only documentation' undersells prototyping, which is about active testing and validation, not just documentation.
'Only coding' misattributes prototyping's purpose to implementation, not design validation.
'Only deployment' misattributes prototyping's purpose to implementation, not design validation.

sampleQuestions.question: Which WCAG principle ensures content is perceivable?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Perceivable covers alternatives and contrast for accessibility.
whyWrong: 'Only operable' misattributes the principle — Operable is a different WCAG principle, not the one about perceivability.
'Only understandable' misattributes the principle — Understandable is a different WCAG principle.
'Only robust' misattributes the principle — Robust is a different WCAG principle, not the one about perceivability.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a design system?
options: Reusable components, patterns, and guidelines for consistent UI
sampleQuestions.explanation: Design systems provide reusable components and guidelines.
whyWrong: A single component doesn't represent the broader reusable system of patterns and guidelines a design system provides.
'Only colors' undersells a design system, which spans components and patterns beyond just color.
'Only typography' undersells a design system, which spans components and patterns beyond just typography.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Experience Cloud capability supports UX Designers?
options: Templates, themes, and declarative site building
sampleQuestions.explanation: Templates, themes, and declarative building support UX design.
whyWrong: 'Only Apex' narrows Experience Cloud's UX capability incorrectly to a single programming language.
'Only APIs' undersells the broader declarative site-building capability being described.
'Only batch' undersells the broader declarative site-building capability being described.

sampleQuestions.question: What does usability testing measure?
options: How effectively users can complete tasks and identify issues
sampleQuestions.explanation: Usability testing measures task completion and identifies issues.
whyWrong: 'Only speed' misattributes usability testing to a performance metric, not task completion effectiveness.
'Only aesthetics' misattributes usability testing to visual design, not task completion effectiveness.
'Only cost' misattributes usability testing to a business metric, not task completion effectiveness.

sampleQuestions.question: Which principle supports inclusive design?
options: Design for diverse abilities and contexts
sampleQuestions.explanation: Inclusive design considers diverse abilities and contexts.
whyWrong: Designing for one user only is the opposite of the inclusive design principle.
'Design for desktop only' is the opposite of the inclusive, diverse-context design principle.
'Design for developers only' misattributes inclusive design's audience, which is end users broadly, not developers.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a user journey map?
options: To visualize user steps, touchpoints, and emotions across an experience
sampleQuestions.explanation: Journey maps visualize user steps and touchpoints.
whyWrong: Journey maps don't replace wireframes — they serve a distinct purpose visualizing the broader experience, not layout structure.
'To write code' misattributes a journey map's purpose to implementation, not experience visualization.
'To deploy' misattributes a journey map's purpose to implementation, not experience visualization.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best practice applies to Lightning Experience design?
options: Design for responsive layouts and Lightning Design System
sampleQuestions.explanation: Responsive design and LDS align with Lightning best practices.
whyWrong: Ignoring mobile contradicts the responsive design best practice for Lightning Experience.
'Desktop only' contradicts the responsive, mobile-inclusive best practice for Lightning Experience design.
'No accessibility' contradicts the fact that accessibility is a core best practice for Lightning Experience design.
